analysis.one_liner: Writes Obama-era offshore oil drilling safety rules into law so they cannot be rolled back.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 64 cosponsors including two Republicans, but the House Natural Resources Committee never acted on it and it died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Safe COAST Act would turn two offshore drilling safety rules — the production safety systems rule and the well control rule, both written after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster — into federal law, so that a future administration could not weaken them through the normal rule-making process. It would also require the Interior Department to finish an independent National Academies review of how offshore rigs are inspected. The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing and tourism economies, and Gulf communities who bear the damage when a well blows out. Under the bill, the safety equipment and procedures required on offshore rigs (blowout preventers, real-time monitoring, well design standards) would be locked into statute as of January 1, 2018, making it far harder for any administration to relax them. The National Academies study would also give Congress and the public an independent look at whether offshore inspections are adequate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and fishing and tourism economies

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the production safety systems rule and the well control rule (30 C.F.R. part 250, subparts D through H and Q, as in effect January 1, 2018) the same force and effect as an Act of Congress, so they could not be repealed or rewritten by a future administration through ordinary rule-making.
These rules govern offshore oil and gas production on the Outer Continental Shelf and provide protections for human, marine, and coastal environments.

The Interior Department would have to contract with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to complete its previously commissioned review of the offshore inspection program within 21 months.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas operators, who would have to keep meeting the 2018 safety equipment and well-control requirements instead of the weaker versions the administration proposed; their compliance costs flow partly into consumers at the margin.

drawbacks.text: Writing the rules into statute as they stood on January 1, 2018 would freeze them: if engineers later found a better or outdated requirement, changing it would take an act of Congress rather than a routine regulatory update.

Offshore operators would bear the cost of maintaining the 2018-level safety systems; industry argues such mandates raise production costs, which can pass through to energy prices, and the bill does not provide any offset.
Re-running the National Academies inspection study on a 21-month clock would add delay before any conclusions about inspection adequacy reach policymakers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is significant and concrete: the rules being codified were written in response to the Deepwater Horizon blowout that killed 11 workers and spilled millions of barrels into the Gulf, and statutory protection prevents the administration then in office from loosening them, which was an active policy direction in 2018. The costs are real but modest — compliance expenses for offshore operators and some rigidity from freezing rules in statute. On balance the design is reasonable; the main weakness is statutory rigidity, which could be addressed with an update mechanism.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Nanette Diaz Barragan introduced the Safe COAST Act on January 29, 2018, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
The bill attracted 64 cosponsors — 62 Democrats and 2 Republicans — within the session.

On January 31, 2018, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources; the congressional record shows no further action, no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

Because the bill was never enacted, the production safety systems rule and well control rule remained ordinary regulations subject to revision by the administration, rather than statutory requirements.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas operators came out ahead: with no law on the books, the safety rules stayed ordinary regulations that the administration could revise, as it proposed to do. Coastal communities gained no statutory protection.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write the offshore safety rules into statute and lined up 64 cosponsors.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan base.

against.what_they_did: The committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was almost entirely Democratic — 62 of its 64 cosponsors — with 2 House Republicans signing on; the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill locks in the 2018 post-Deepwater Horizon safety requirements, ending the industry's prospects of a rollback of the production safety systems and well control rules. Its gain from the bill dying — cheaper, looser regulation — is the public's loss in spill and blowout risk borne by coastal residents.

Stronger statutory safety rules lower the chance of a spill like Deepwater Horizon, which devastated Gulf fishing and tourism for years. These businesses profit from the same protections ordinary coastal residents want.

industries.industry: Offshore oilfield service and equipment suppliers
industries.note: Mandated safety systems mean equipment sales (blowout preventers, monitoring technology), but codified rules could also reduce demand for newer systems as operators stick with the frozen 2018 standard.
